name: Tanuz Kalita
project: Indigenous Youth Led Habitat Restoration for Climate Resilience in Majuli
deck: Majuli loses land to the Brahmaputra every year. Three thousand native saplings went into the erosion-prone banks, and fifty kilos of weaving thread went to the households that live on them.
description: Three thousand native saplings into the eroding banks at Salmora and Karatipar, and fifty kilos of weaving thread to the households living on them.

aims.p: Restore the erosion-prone stretches at Salmora and Karatipar with native species — arjuna, simolu, elephant apple — rather than whatever grows fastest.
Indigenous youth learn the restoration work and the weaving both, because a livelihood is what makes anyone stay to water a sapling.
Trees a household earns from are trees that are still alive in year two. That is the whole argument for putting thread and saplings in the same project.

did: Mobilised communities across several Majuli villages and picked the planting sites with them
Planted 3,000 native saplings — arjuna, simolu and elephant apple
Distributed 50 kg of indigenous weaving thread to participating households
Ran youth training in ecological restoration and in weaving — thirty to forty young implementers, alongside ten to fifteen local experts
Held plantation drives and awareness sessions in the riverside villages

quotes.text: With the threads we received, we can continue our weaving and earn more from it. It helps us support our families while keeping our traditional designs and skills alive.
quotes.speaker: Manisha Payeng

quotes.text: These saplings will help protect our land from erosion. We have seen how the river takes away our soil every year, and planting these native trees gives us some hope for the future.
quotes.speaker: Banajit Doley

quotes.text: This work is important for our community. The saplings will help reduce erosion in Majuli, and at the same time, weaving support is giving our youth and women a way to earn while keeping our traditions alive.
quotes.speaker: A volunteer in Karatipar, Majuli

frames.alt: Three women crouched on open grassland pressing loose earth around newly planted saplings, six more standing behind them in bright mekhela sador, one holding a curved blade and another a bare-rooted sapling with its ball of soil
